newsitem.title: CROATIA: Leading Croatian bank to change its "dated" image.
newsitem.headline: Leading Croatian bank to change its "dated" image.

text.p: Zagrebacka Banka, the leading Croatian commercial bank, said on Thursday it would lay off workers, cut expenses and change its "dated" image and way of working with clients by the end of the century.

"The old way of working in Zagrebacka did not change much in the past seven years: the counters look dated, we still have a dated attitude towards the clients and a dated, numerous work force," board member Davor Holjevac told a banking conference.
Holjevac said the bank planned to re-design the interior of some 150 bank branches across the country.
He gave no details as to how many people were to be made redundant, or by when.

Zagrebacka is the only Croatian bank fully listed on the Zagreb Stock Exchange and Seaq International in London, where its 1/10 Global Depositary Receipts traded in a $29.75-$29.515 range on Wednesday.
The bank is also in the process of getting a credit rating, and is planning to issue its own Eurobonds later this month or in early April, Holjevac said.
He said the bank was aiming to secure one third of the Croatian market in terms of business with citizens by 2000 -- its share in 1996 was estimated at 29 percent.
At the same time its share in the domestic foreign currency market is expected to drop to 40 from 42 percent last year.

"Some might regard this projection as too pessimistic, some as too optimistic," Holjevac said, adding that competition of foreign banks -- eyeing particularly this lucrative segment of the market -- was toughening.
Zagrebacka would like to see itself 32 percent-owned by foreign investors by 2000, up from 23.89 percent in December 1996, Holjevac said.
Its share of state-owned firms and public funds was at the same time expected to fall to 13 percent from over 24 percent now.
In terms of credit policy, the bank plans to intensify lending to individuals at the expense of firms.
The share of individual loans in its total credit potential is expected to rise to 30 percent from a current 18, while loans to firms are charted to fall to around 65 from the current 78 percent.

Holjevac said the bank's high profile abroad and cheaper credit lines, not available to smaller players on the Croatian financial market, would potentially enable it to play a role of creditor of small and middle-size banks.

"There are definitely too many banks on the Croatian market; there is no place for all 61 of them," Holjevac said, adding that acquisitions by bigger banks and mergers would inevitably follow in the next few years.
